7	SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.
8	
9	**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.
10	
11	**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
12	- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
13	- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
14	- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).
15	
16	**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
17	- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
18	- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
19	- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
20	- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
21	- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
22	- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
23	- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
24	- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.
25	
26	**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

7	**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.
8	
9	**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.
10	
11	Key phase 3 concepts:
12	- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
13	- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
14	- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
15	- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
16	- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
17	- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
18	- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
19	- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
20	- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
21	- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
22	- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.
23	
24	**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.
25	
26	**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

## Project shape

SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor + execution engine at `/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/`. Three independent programs share a map directory: server (file CRUD HTTP proxy), runner (sync Lua executor in phase 2 → C pool runner in phase 3), and the vanilla-JS canvas editor in `assets/`. Phase 1 complete, phase 2 in active development, phase 3 fully designed across issues 301–313 but not built.

Box files are individual JSONs in `maps/<map>/boxes/<id>.json`. Single output wire per box (issue 218). Iterators and comparators are routing primitives. Phase 2 uses shell-script drivers; phase 3 will use `.so` language specs via `dlopen` with Unix-domain-socket out-of-process specs for bash. SoraMech owns its own C thread pool (3d-rts as design reference only, not vendored). Effil and coroutines are explicitly not used.

40	The editor is editor-only — no run button, no run results display.
41	The runner is invoked separately, by command line. `last-run.jsonl`
42	(issue 311) is the runner's output, consumed by external tooling, not
43	by the editor.
44	
45	### Phase 2 runner — `src/007-runner-main.lua`
46	
47	Synchronous Lua interpreter. Loads a map directory, validates the
48	graph, walks boxes in dependency order, invokes language drivers per
49	box (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/c.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`). Each box
50	invocation is wrapped in a `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` boundary that
51	matches the phase 3 thread pool's action signature.
52	
53	This is the development target while the editor is being built out.
54	
55	### Phase 3 runner — `soramech-pool` (planned, issues 301–311)
56	
57	C binary that owns a SoraMech-built thread pool (3d-rts is the
58	design reference, not vendored). Each box invocation is a pool
59	task; worker threads run them concurrently. Language code is
60	called through **language specs** (issue 303), shared libraries
61	(`langs/<name>/spec.so`) loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Lua and C
62	specs are in-process; the Bash spec talks to a persistent
63	subprocess over a Unix domain socket. Wire values live in
64	**per-input-port slots** in process heap memory (issue 302) — ring
65	buffers durable for the run, plus a large-value heap for
66	variable-size payloads.
67	
68	Phase 3 replaces the phase 2 runner wholesale. The synchronous path
69	does not survive into phase 3; the editor and the map directory
70	format are unchanged across the cutover.
71	
72	### assets/index.html (the editor)
73	
74	Static HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.
75	Talks to `src/006-server-main.lua` for all file operations. No run
76	button, no compile button (yet — issue 222 adds a placeholder
77	"Compile" button as part of phase 2). The runner is invoked
78	separately.
79	
80	## Map directory format
81	
82	```
83	maps/<name>/
84	  meta.json          — { name, description, entry_box_id, src_dirs?, lang? }
85	  boxes/
86	    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)
87	  data/
88	    <name>.json      — Lua table as JSON; sections have "constant": bool
89	  src/
90	    *.lua, *.c, *.sh — box function source files
91	  compiled/          — produced by the compile button (issue 222)
92	    pool-runner      — the compiled C entry point for this map
93	    src/             — copy of every source file the map uses
94	    bin/             — compiled .so files (C boxes via the C language spec)
95	    manifest.json    — every box, its language, its compiled artifact path
96	  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/
97	    last-run.json    — phase 2 run snapshot (single document)
98	    last-run.jsonl   — phase 3 run log (JSON Lines, issue 311)
99	    logs/            — additional run logs
100	```
101	
102	Note: the phase 2 `drivers.json` file is gone. Language selection in
103	phase 2 is by file extension via the `drivers/` directory; in phase 3
104	the spec registry resolves languages by `box.lang` against
105	`langs/<name>/spec.so` — no map-local config file needed.
106	
107	## Box file format
108	
109	```json
110	{
111	  "id": "trim",
112	  "label": "Trim whitespace",
113	  "kind": "call",
114	  "lang": "lua",
115	  "ref": "src/strings.lua",
116	  "fn": "trim",
117	  "inputs": [
118	    { "name": "text", "type": "string" }
119	  ],
120	  "output_capacity": 4096,
121	  "connections": [
122	    {
123	      "from_box": "trim",
124	      "from_branch": null,
125	      "to_box": "next-box-id",
126	      "to_input": "text"
127	    }
128	  ],
129	  "ui": { "x": 120, "y": 340 }
130	}
131	```
132	
133	Every box has exactly **one output wire**. There is no `outputs`
134	array. Whatever the function returns travels down the single output
135	wire as one value (issue 218). Multiple values that need to travel
136	together are encoded as JSON or a struct and decoded downstream.
137	
138	`output_capacity` declares the maximum number of bytes the slot
139	allocator (issue 302) reserves for the output. `0` (or omitted) means
140	variable-size — the slot stores a handle into the large-value heap.
141	
142	### Comparator boxes
143	A box may carry a `comparand` field (a literal number as a string).
144	When set, the dispatch layer compares the input value to the
145	comparand and fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches
146	`"lt"` / `"eq"` / `"gt"`. Comparators have no `ref` / `fn` — the
147	routing logic lives in the dispatch layer (issue 304). The output
148	slot carries the input value through unchanged.
149	
150	```json
151	{
152	  "id": "classify",
153	  "kind": "call",
154	  "comparand": "0",
155	  "inputs": [{ "name": "value", "type": "number" }],
156	  "connections": [
157	    { "from_box": "classify", "from_branch": "lt", "to_box": "negative", "to_input": "n" },
158	    { "from_box": "classify", "from_branch": "eq", "to_box": "zero",     "to_input": "n" },
159	    { "from_box": "classify", "from_branch": "gt", "to_box": "positive", "to_input": "n" }
160	  ]
161	}
162	```
163	
164	The earlier `branch` box kind with named ports is removed (see issue
165	210). Comparator + `from_branch` is the only branching mechanism.
166	
167	### Iterator boxes
168	A box may carry an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of
169	output slot names. The dispatch layer routes the input value to the
170	slot named `iterator_outputs[counter]`, advances the counter (mod
171	length), and re-spawns itself to consume the next queued input. No
172	function is invoked — iterators are pure routing primitives. Issue
173	221 covers the model; 213 covers the queued-input semantics.
174	
175	### Connections
176	Connections are written to BOTH endpoint box files. The runner
177	validates at load time that both ends agree. Disagreement is a hard
178	error.
179	
180	```json
181	{ "from_box": "...", "from_branch": null|"lt"|"eq"|"gt"|"<iter-slot>",
182	  "to_box": "...",   "to_input": "..." }
183	```
184	
185	`from_branch` is `null` for plain call boxes (single output wire).
186	
187	## Language spec system (phase 3)
188	
189	Each language is a **spec** — a `.so` library at
190	`langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` symbol with
191	`init` / `teardown` / `compile` / `invoke` callbacks. The pool runner
192	loads every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup via `dlopen`. The spec
193	contract (issue 303) is uniform across languages; no language is
194	privileged.
195	
196	Reference specs ship with SoraMech:
197	- `langs/lua/spec.so` — in-process via `lua_State`, no compile step (issue 306)
198	- `langs/c/spec.so`   — in-process via `dlopen`, with a compile step that generates a wrapper (issue 307)
199	- `langs/bash/spec.so`— out-of-process via Unix domain socket to a persistent subprocess (issue 308)
200	
201	A user adds a new language (Python, Rust, anything) by writing a new
202	spec under `langs/<name>/`. SoraMech itself does not transpile or
203	convert source between languages.
204	
205	The phase 2 `drivers/*.sh` scripts retire when phase 3 lands. They
206	implement the same idea (one process per call, stdout as channel)
207	that the spec system replaces with persistent runtimes and
208	length-prefix-framed sockets / direct function pointers.
209	
210	## Execution model — phase 2 (synchronous)
211	
212	The runner walks the graph depth-first from the entry box. Each box
213	call:
214	
215	1. Collect inputs: read wired output values from predecessor boxes.
216	2. Invoke driver: shell out to the appropriate driver script.
217	3. Collect output: decode single JSON value from driver stdout.
218	4. Store output: held in runner memory, keyed by box id.
219	5. Fire connections: enqueue boxes whose input dependencies are now
220	   met.
221	
222	Each step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be
223	swapped for the phase 3 pool runner without changing the box
224	execution model. Phase 2 is single-threaded.
225	
226	## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)
227	
228	The C pool runner owns a SoraMech-built thread pool with N worker
229	threads (3d-rts is the design reference, not vendored). Each box
230	invocation is a task. The dispatch layer (issue 304) is the
231	worker-side action: read inputs from slots → branch on box mode
232	→ invoke the language spec (or route directly, for comparators /
233	iterators) → push output to downstream input slots.
234	
235	Slots are **per-input-port** ring buffers (issue 302), allocated
236	at graph load and durable for the run. 1-cell slots use peek
237	(literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop (multi-push
238	wires, queues from iterators). Iterator counter is per-box state,
239	incremented atomically at task spawn time so iterator tasks can
240	parallelize across workers; pushes carry counter tags so consumer
241	slots preserve invocation order. Run termination is governed by
242	the pool's active-task counter — when it hits zero with no
243	pending spawns, the run is over.
244	
245	The pool runner has no embedded Lua. It is C from `main` down to the
246	language spec boundary; only inside a Lua spec's `invoke` does Lua
247	code run, and only inside that worker's `lua_State`. The graph
248	loader is also pure C (issue 305) — phase 2's
249	`src/003-loader.lua` retires.
250	
251	See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` for the full IPC and threading
252	discussion, including the blocking-semantics constraint on long-
253	running operations.
254	
255	## Data files
256	
257	Persistent data lives in `data/<name>.json`. Format:
258	
259	```json
260	{
261	  "constant": false,
262	  "fields": {
263	    "history": [],
264	    "config": { "constant": true, "value": { "model": "soramind-default" } }
265	  }
266	}
267	```
268	
269	Top-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only.
270	Individual fields can be flagged constant within an otherwise
271	mutable file. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
272	
273	Ephemeral state (scratch tables, run logs, the `last-run.jsonl`
274	output) goes to `tmp/`, a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Survives
275	the run but not a reboot — intentionally.
276	
```

1	# 233 — Unified `routing` schema for branching boxes
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Concept
7	
8	A "branching box" is a regular call box whose output, after the
9	function runs, is sent to **one of several** downstream
10	destinations rather than to all of them. Same function, same
11	inputs, same output value — only the routing decision differs.
12	Currently we have two flavors:
13	
14	- **Comparator**: routes the function's output by comparing it
15	  to a stored threshold. Three fixed branches (`lt` / `eq` /
16	  `gt`).
17	- **Iterator**: routes the function's output to one of N branches
18	  in round-robin fashion, advancing a counter on every call.
19	
20	The two are the same shape (function runs → output gets routed)
21	with different rules for picking the branch. The current schema
22	has them as separate top-level fields (`comparand` and
23	`iterator_outputs`), which makes them look like unrelated
24	features. They aren't.
25	
26	(For "send the same value to multiple destinations," the user
27	just pulls multiple wires out of a single output port — fan-out
28	already works on plain call boxes. No routing decision needed.)
29	
30	### Branch-level fan-out
31	
32	Fan-out applies on a per-branch basis even for branched boxes. If
33	the comparator's `lt` port has three wires going to three
34	different consumers, then each time the routing decision picks
35	`lt`, all three wires receive the value (a copy is pushed into
36	each consumer's input slot). On a subsequent invocation that
37	picks `eq`, only the wires hanging off the `eq` port fire.
38	
39	Each branch port acts like its own little plain-call output port
40	when it fires. The routing decision picks **which branch** fires;
41	the branch's own fan-out picks **which consumers** receive the
42	value when it does.
43	
44	## Intended behavior
45	
46	Every call box carries a `routing` field. No implicit defaulting:
47	plain boxes have `routing: { "kind": "plain" }`, the same way
48	branched boxes carry their own kind. Explicit and consistent —
49	no "what if I forget the routing field" surprises at validation
50	time.
51	
52	```json
53	{ "id": "plain-call",
54	  "kind": "call",
55	  "ref": "...", "fn": "...",
56	  "inputs": [...],
57	  "routing": { "kind": "plain" } }
58	
59	{ "id": "score-router",
60	  "kind": "call",
61	  "ref": "src/score.lua", "fn": "score",
62	  "inputs": [...],
63	  "routing": { "kind": "comparator", "comparand": 4 } }
64	
65	{ "id": "round-robin",
66	  "kind": "call",
67	  "ref": "src/dispatch_msg.lua", "fn": "dispatch_msg",
68	  "routing": { "kind": "iterator", "n_outputs": 3 } }
69	```
70	
71	Routing kinds defined in this design: `plain`, `comparator`,
72	`iterator`, `randomizer`, `weighted`, `distributor`. Of those,
73	**this issue ships `plain`, `comparator`, and `iterator` only**
74	— that's the surface area already in production, just unified
75	under one schema. The other three (`randomizer`, `weighted`,
76	`distributor`) are designed below for context but split into
77	their own follow-on issue files when this one is implemented, so
78	each ships independently.
79	
80	The `routing.kind` field picks which dispatch-layer rule decides
81	the branch. Schema validates the kind value and the kind-specific
82	parameters together.
83	
84	**The function always runs**, regardless of routing kind. The
85	function produces the value; routing decides where the value
86	goes.
87	
88	### kind="plain"
89	
90	```json
91	"routing": { "kind": "plain" }
92	```
93	
94	One output port. The function's output value fans to every wire
95	attached to that port unconditionally. No routing decision; the
96	dispatch layer skips the branch picker and pushes to all wires.
97	
98	This is the default for new boxes; the editor sets it
99	automatically when a box is created.
100	
101	### kind="comparator"
102	
103	```json
104	"routing": { "kind": "comparator", "comparand": "<number>" }
105	```
106	
107	Three output ports: `lt`, `eq`, `gt` (fixed names; ports aren't
108	renameable per the editor's port-immutability rule). The
109	function's output value is compared to `comparand`; the matching
110	branch fires.
111	
112	#### Multi-band comparator (planned brainstorm)
113	
114	The current 3-branch lt/eq/gt design is a special case of "value
115	falls into a numeric range, fire the corresponding branch." A
116	generalization:
117	
118	```json
119	"routing": {
120	  "kind": "comparator",
121	  "thresholds": [3, 7, 11, 17]
122	}
123	```
124	
125	Five output ports get named by the threshold positions —
126	`below_3`, `between_3_7`, `between_7_11`, `between_11_17`,
127	`above_17`. With `thresholds: [4]` this becomes the current
128	3-branch lt/eq/gt (with `eq` being "exactly 4"), so the legacy
129	shape is one configuration of the new one.
130	
131	**Equality bands via doubled thresholds.** Encode the current
132	`eq` semantics by repeating a threshold value: `thresholds: [3, 3]`
133	means "less than 3, exactly 3, greater than 3" — three bands, the
134	middle one being a zero-width point that fires only on exact
135	equality. With `thresholds: [3, 3, 7, 7]` you get five bands:
136	`< 3`, `== 3`, `3 < x < 7`, `== 7`, `> 7`. The editor sees a
137	list of thresholds; the runtime sees doubled values as
138	"point bands."
139	
140	This means the legacy 3-branch lt/eq/gt is exactly
141	`thresholds: [c, c]` — the eq case is just a zero-width band at
142	the comparand. Behind the scenes the editor can present the
143	single-comparand UI but store `[c, c]` so the dispatch layer has
144	one consistent representation.
145	
146	Defer the schema specifics — the single-comparand case ships
147	first; multi-band is a follow-on once we have a use case that
148	actually needs more than three.
149	
150	### kind="iterator"
151	
152	```json
153	"routing": { "kind": "iterator", "n_outputs": 3 }
154	```
155	
156	`n_outputs` output ports, named conventionally (`out_0`, `out_1`,
157	…). Every invocation reads the box's `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot
158	via `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`; that index picks
159	the branch.
160	
161	The function still runs and produces the routed value. Iterator
162	defaults the function to a passthrough identity if the user
163	hasn't picked a `ref` / `fn` — but the user is free to attach
164	any function whose output should be round-robin-distributed.
165	
166	### kind="randomizer"
167	
168	```json
169	"routing": { "kind": "randomizer", "n_outputs": 4 }
170	```
171	
172	Picks a branch uniformly at random per invocation.
173	Implementation: hash the counter-slot value into the branch
174	index, so the distribution is deterministic-given-seed but
175	spread across branches.
176	
177	```c
178	uint32_t i = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, UINT32_MAX);
179	uint32_t branch = hash(i) % n_outputs;
180	```
181	
182	`hash` is a cheap mixing function (xorshift, FNV); not
183	cryptographic. The point is breaking up the monotonic counter so
184	consecutive calls don't go to consecutive branches.
185	
186	### kind="weighted"
187	
188	```json
189	"routing": {
190	  "kind":    "weighted",
191	  "weights": [0.8, 0.2]
192	}
193	```
194	
195	Probability-based distribution. With `[0.8, 0.2]` and two output
196	ports, 80% of invocations fire branch 0, 20% fire branch 1.
197	
198	Implementation: at compile time, weights are normalized into a
199	cumulative table on a `0..PRECISION-1` integer scale (e.g.

202	```c

204	// pre-computed cumulative: [0..799] → branch 0, [800..999] → branch 1
205	uint32_t branch = lookup_band(r, cumulative_table);
206	```

230	```json

234	Sends the value to the **least-busy** downstream consumer:
235	inspects the fill levels of the input slots wired to each branch

239	Implementation: dispatch action peeks the `tail - head` count on

244	This is the only routing kind that's not purely
245	self-contained — it reads downstream slot state — but it doesn't

251	The pattern is: any new routing kind plugs in at one place

253	existing kinds and any future ones live entirely in the dispatch

257	## Iterator + function: ships as "function always runs"
258	
259	Iterator boxes always run their function. The dispatch action
260	becomes uniform across routing kinds:
261	
262	```
263	1. Read inputs (pop / peek per port mode).
264	2. Invoke spec (always — function runs regardless of routing kind).
265	3. Pick branch via routing.kind:
266	     comparator   → compare(output, comparand)
267	     iterator     → slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)
268	     randomizer   → hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % n_outputs
269	     weighted     → cumulative lookup
270	     distributor  → argmin(downstream fill)
271	     (no routing) → fan to all outgoing wires
272	4. Push function output to outputs[picked branch] (or all wires if
273	   no routing).
274	```
275	
276	A single dispatch path for all branching boxes; the routing rule
277	plugs into step 3.

363	- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — counter slot mechanism
364	  used by iterator / randomizer / weighted

366	  picker dispatches on `routing.kind`

370	- **Distributor under fan-out**: if a branch wire goes to
371	  multiple consumers (fan-out), the "fill level" of that branch

378	- **Weighted ties**: floating-point weights summing to `1.0`
379	  doesn't always discretize cleanly. Compile-time normalization
380	  picks an integer scale (1000) and rounds; the last band
381	  absorbs any leftover so the ranges always sum to PRECISION.

384	
385	The big follow-on after this issue ships is a fully data-driven
386	router: one dispatch path that reads a small rule expression

388	
389	```json
390	"routing": {
391	  "kind": "rules",
392	  "rules": [
393	    { "when": "output < 3",                   "to": "small" },
394	    { "when": "output >= 3 and output < 7",   "to": "medium" },
395	    { "when": "output >= 7",                  "to": "large" }
396	  ]
397	}
398	```
399	
400	The dispatch layer ships a small expression evaluator (a few
401	dozen lines: variables = `output`, `counter`, `fill[i]`;
402	operators = comparisons, boolean conjunction, arithmetic). Every
403	existing routing kind reduces to a "rules" expression:
404	
405	- comparator → three rules with `when: output < c / output == c / output > c`
406	- iterator → one rule using `counter % N` as the band index
407	- randomizer → one rule using `hash(counter) % N`
408	- weighted → cumulative-band rules
409	
410	The benefit: one code path in dispatch instead of five. Custom
411	routing without writing a spec callback or modifying user
412	functions. The cost: a small evaluator (still entirely in C, no
413	spec involvement).
414	
415	Worth pursuing once Level B has shipped and we have real maps
416	using the kinds — at that point the consolidation is concrete
417	rather than speculative. Open as a separate issue when ready.

1	# 229 — Data box: a language-agnostic file source (and a paired file sink)
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	The `data` kind is recognized by the schema (`call` and `data` are
9	the two valid kinds) and accepted by the loader, but it has no
10	runtime semantics distinct from `call`. It carries a `ref` and an
11	`fn` like a call box and runs through whichever language driver
12	matches the file extension. The only difference is the green badge
13	on the canvas — pure cosmetic.
14	
15	A user reading the editor reasonably expects `data` to mean "read
16	some data, emit it" — "if it walks like a duck…" — but the current
17	implementation doesn't deliver that. `libs/files.lua::read_text`
18	covers the actual "read a text file" need (issue 216, complete) via
19	a regular call box.
20	
21	## Intended behavior
22	
23	Repurpose the `data` kind into a **language-agnostic file source**.
24	A data box has:
25	- `ref` — an absolute or map-relative path to a file on disk.
26	- **No `fn`** — the dispatch layer is the function.
27	- **No inputs** — emits whenever its successors fire.
28	- A single output wire carrying the file's contents.
29	
30	The runtime reads the file at the dispatch layer, encodes the bytes
31	as a string (UTF-8), and pushes the value onto the output wire. No
32	language driver is invoked. Same shape as the iterator box (issue
33	221): kind says "call," presence of a routing field marks the box
34	as a primitive the dispatch layer handles directly.
35	
36	### Why language-agnostic matters
37	
38	A user writing a Bash function that needs file contents shouldn't
39	have to wire through a Lua read box — and vice versa. A file's
40	bytes are a string; every language consumes a string; the
41	read-and-emit step has no language-specific anything. Pulling it
42	into the dispatch layer makes it available identically from every
43	language.
44	
45	It also keeps the graph readable: a user reading a map sees
46	`config.json → parse → ...` and immediately knows where the data
47	came from. The current alternative — a call box pointing at
48	`files.read_text` — works but adds a layer of indirection that
49	buries what the user is doing.
50	
51	### Paired sink: `kind: "sink"` (or similar) for writing files
52	
53	The complement is a language-agnostic file sink. A user wires a
54	string into it; the dispatch layer writes the string to the
55	configured path. Inputs:
56	- `path` (string) — destination on disk
57	- `text` (string) — content to write
58	
59	No outputs (per issue 226's sink semantics). No `ref` or `fn`. The
60	kind name needs picking — `sink` is taken metaphorically already;
61	`file_write` is unambiguous; `write` is short. Defer the bikeshed.
62	
63	Both the source and the sink atomic-write where it matters: write
64	to `path.tmp`, fsync, rename to `path`. Standard pattern; matches
65	how `soramech-data` handles its writes.
66	
67	### Schema
68	
69	For the source:
70	```json
71	{
72	  "id": "config",
73	  "kind": "data",
74	  "path": "config.json",
75	  "ui": { "x": 100, "y": 100 }
76	}
77	```

79	`ref` is gone — repurposed as `path` so the field name says what it

81	a function at this ref). Inputs are absent; outputs are absent (the
82	single-output rule still gives one wire).
83	
84	For the sink, the kind name TBD; data layout:
85	```json
86	{
87	  "id": "save",
88	  "kind": "file_write",
89	  "inputs": [
90	    {"name": "path",  "type": "string"},
91	    {"name": "text",  "type": "string"}
92	  ],
93	  "ui": { "x": 100, "y": 100 }
94	}
95	```

98	paths upstream (e.g. by a function that builds a timestamped name).
99	Could also add an optional `path` field for the static case where
100	the user just wants a file written to a fixed location.
101	
102	### Concerns about language-agnostic file IO
103	
104	The original "data files have language semantics" concern (paraphrasing
105	from prior conversations: "different languages store strings
106	differently") doesn't apply here. The runtime owns the read/write,
107	not any language; it always emits bytes-as-UTF-8 string and always
108	accepts the same shape on the way in. Languages each receive a
109	plain string from the wire and turn it into whatever their native
110	string type is — that conversion is already part of the language

126	The user asked whether parsing should happen in the data box or in

1	# 230 — Required inputs, the optional flag, and no-null-from-missing
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	A box's input port can be left without a wire and without a literal
9	value. The phase 2 executor runs the box anyway; the function on
10	the other end gets `nil` (Lua), unset (Bash), or whatever default
11	the language hands a missing positional arg. Errors only surface if
12	the function happens to reference the missing arg in a way the
13	language can't tolerate (e.g. `string.upper(nil)` in Lua).
14	
15	This is a class of silent-error bug. The user had a wiring intent,
16	forgot to plug something in, and the runtime quietly papered over
17	the mistake.
18	
19	## Intended behavior
20	
21	Every input port is in one of three states by **compile time**:
22	
23	1. A wire is connected to it.
24	2. A literal value is set on it.
25	3. It carries `optional: true` on the port record.
26	
27	**Compile fails** when any port is in none of those states. The
28	error is precise: which box, which port. The Compile button (issue
29	222) is the natural enforcement point, with the same check
30	duplicating in the phase 3 graph loader (issue 305).
31	
32	### "Optional" is not "null"
33	
34	`optional: true` says "this argument doesn't have to be passed." It
35	does not mean "pass null." At the spec boundary, an optional
36	unwired un-littered port produces a shorter arg list — the language
37	sees fewer arguments, not a null argument. Each language handles
38	that natively:
39	
40	- **Lua**: omitted args are `nil`. That's a language convention,
41	  not a wire-level value. Inside the Lua function, `arg or default`
42	  works.
43	- **Bash**: a positional arg that wasn't passed is unset.
44	  `${arg:-default}` provides a default.
45	- **C**: the spec's compile callback (issue 307) generates a wrapper
46	  that reads `n_inputs` and only forwards the args that are present.
47	
48	### Null as an explicit value (allowed)
49	
50	If the user needs to pass null because some downstream library
51	expects it, they can — by typing the literal `null` into the value
52	field. That's a string on the wire encoded as JSON null. Each spec
53	maps it to its language's native null on the way in:
54	
55	| JSON value  | Lua    | Bash       | C       |
56	|-------------|--------|------------|---------|
57	| `null`      | nil    | empty `""` | `NULL`  |
58	| `42`        | 42     | `"42"`     | 42      |
59	| `"foo"`     | `foo`  | `foo`      | `"foo"` |
60	| `true`      | true   | `"true"`   | `1`     |
61	
62	The crucial distinction: **explicit null arrives through the
63	function call as a real argument**; **optional-and-absent does not
64	arrive at all**. Bash empty-string-vs-unset disappears in the
65	optional path because the arg position simply isn't passed.
66	
67	### Schema
68	
69	Add `optional` as an optional boolean on input port records:
70	
71	```json
72	{
73	  "name": "config_path",
74	  "type": "string",
75	  "optional": true
76	}
77	```
78	
79	Absence means `false`. No migration; existing maps work unchanged.
80	
81	## Compile-time check
82	
83	The check walks every box, every input. For each:
84	- If the port has `value` set (literal): pass.
85	- If any connection has `to_box === box.id && to_input === port.name`:
86	  pass.
87	- If `port.optional === true`: pass.
88	- Otherwise: error, with a precise message:
89	  `"box <id>: input '<port>' has no wire, no literal, and is not optional"`
90	
91	The check runs:
92	- **Editor** — on Compile button click (issue 222 → 309). Errors
93	  surface in the editor without writing the compiled output.
94	- **Loader** — at run time (phase 3 issue 305). Errors abort the
95	  run. Belt and suspenders: the editor catches it but a hand-edited
96	  map JSON can still trip the loader check.
97	
98	## Spec API for "is this arg present?"
99	
100	The spec doesn't need to ask. The dispatch layer assembles
101	`input_data[]` and `input_sizes[]` from the slots that actually
102	have values. An optional port that's absent isn't in those arrays;
103	`n_inputs` is shorter by one. The spec invokes the language with
104	the args it received. The language's native call convention does
105	the rest.
106	
107	For C specifically, the compile-callback-generated wrapper takes
108	`int n_inputs` and a count-prefixed array. The wrapper picks the
109	first M args that match its declared parameters and forwards them;
110	trailing optionals get omitted from the call (or filled with C's
111	zero-valued types, depending on the wrapper convention). This is
112	issue 307's territory.
113	
114	## Inspector UI
115	
116	A small per-port flag in the inspector's port block:
117	
118	```
119	[name] [var] [opt]
120	[ value ........... ]
121	```
122	
123	`opt` toggles `port.optional` on the port record. Visual: same
124	small button as `var` but distinct color.
125	
126	## Open questions
127	
128	- **Whether to allow optional + literal**: yes. A literal is an
129	  explicit value; the optional flag is irrelevant when the value
130	  is set. The compile check just needs all three signals
131	  available; literal wins over optional.
132	- **What syntax means "explicit null literal"**: lean toward
133	  literally typing `null` (case-insensitive) in the value field.
134	  An ambiguity arises when the user actually wants the string
135	  `"null"` — escape it as `"null"` (with quotes) which the value
136	  parser interprets as a string literal. Worth nailing down before
137	  shipping.
138	
139	## Relevant files
140	
141	- `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `optional` field
142	- `src/003-loader.lua` (phase 2) — compile-time check
143	- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — `opt` toggle in port block
144	- `assets/js/005-app.js` — Compile button hooks check before
145	  compile
146	- `issues/309-build-system.md` — compile/package step calls the
147	  check
148	- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — phase 3 check at load time
149	- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke`'s n_inputs
150	  reflects what was actually passed
151	- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — wrapper handles short-arg case
152	- `issues/308-bash-language-spec.md` — null vs unset distinction
153	  evaporates in the optional path
154

### Tool result

```
1	# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	Wire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values
8	have no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language
9	accessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.
10	
11	## Concept
12	
13	### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks
14	
15	Each box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph
16	loads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing
17	declaration: "the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value
18	into this consumer's named input slot." The producer never owns a
19	slot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.
20	
21	When a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into
22	every downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N
23	pushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into
24	the same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same
25	push-into-input-slot mechanic.
26	
27	Slots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker
28	thread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs
29	(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot
30	addresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not
31	shared memory.
32	
33	### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable
34	
35	A **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's
36	input slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every
37	downstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're
38	just stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the
39	dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot
40	holds at least one value).
41	
42	The **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any
43	counter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so
44	on. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and
45	go.
46	
47	This is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N
48	times where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply
49	(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the
50	task does:
51	- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the
52	  return to outputs.
53	- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to
54	  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.
55	  No spec invocation.
56	- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare
57	  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /
58	  `eq` / `gt` branch.
59	
60	### All slots are ring buffers; read mode varies
61	
62	There is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,
63	each of `cell_capacity` bytes. The number of cells (`n_cells`) and
64	the read mode are both compile-time properties of the input port:
65	
66	- **1-cell + peek mode**: the value the producer wrote stays in the
67	  cell. Tasks read via `slot_peek` — read without draining — and
68	  every subsequent task on this consumer reads the same value
69	  unless the producer overwrites it. Used for **single-push wires**
70	  (a literal, or a wire from a producer box whose invocation count
71	  is exactly 1). Multiple consumer tasks read the value as many
72	  times as needed; the cell is never empty.
73	- **N-cell + pop mode**: a queue. Producers push; consumers
74	  `slot_pop` — drain one cell per task. Used for **multi-push wires**:
75	  any wire whose producer has more than one task invocation
76	  during the run. The producer's pushes accumulate, the consumer
77	  drains in pop order.
78	
79	Compile-time analysis classifies each wire. A producer is
80	"runs-once" if no transitive ancestor is an iterator; otherwise
81	it's "runs-N-times." Wires from runs-once producers get 1-cell
82	peek slots; wires from runs-N-times producers get N-cell pop slots.
83	
84	`n_cells` for pop slots is sized for worst-case backlog (or a
85	default like 64 with growth on demand). Lists grow if the producer
86	outruns the consumer past the pre-allocation.
87	
88	Fan-in: multiple producers pushing into the same N-cell pop slot
89	land in arrival order. The consumer pops FIFO unless the cell
90	carries an ordering tag (see "Cell tagging" below).
91	
92	### Atomic-counter slot mode
93	
94	A slot allocated with `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` carries a single
95	4-byte unsigned integer cell, read via a special op:
96	
97	```c
98	uint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);
99	// Returns the current value mod `mod`, then atomically increments
100	// the underlying counter. Concurrent readers each get a distinct
101	// value. Counter wraps at 2^32; mod handles N-branch routing.
102	```
103	
104	Used for iterator counters (issue 304): the iterator box has an
105	auto-allocated `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot at load time; the
106	dispatch action calls `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_branches)`
107	to pick its output branch. Multiple iterator tasks can read
108	concurrently from the same counter slot in parallel — each gets a
109	unique routing index — without any per-box mutable state and
110	without the serial dependency of a self-push counter.
111	
112	The slot's "cell" is just an `atomic_uint32_t`. No push is ever
113	performed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's
114	perspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's
115	perspective the read op is special-cased.
116	
117	### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)
118	
119	A cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its
120	size and data:
121	
122	```
123	Cell layout (N-cell pop slot)
124	Offset  Size  Field
125	------  ----  -----
126	0       4     filled_size
127	4       4     tag      (0 if untagged; iterator counter snapshot otherwise)
128	8       …     data
129	```
130	
131	Slots created for wires from parallel iterators (issue 304) are
132	tagged. Pop on a tagged slot returns the cell with the lowest tag,
133	not the head cell — preserving iterator-counter order across pushes
134	that arrived out of order from parallel iterator workers.
135	
136	Untagged slots default tag to 0 and pop FIFO at no extra cost. The
137	tag-aware pop is a per-slot mode flag set at allocation time.
138	
139	### Asynchrony
140	The store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and
141	freed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization
142	is per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.
143	
144	## Slot layout
145	
146	Each slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`
147	bytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:
148	
149	```
150	Slot header
151	Offset  Size  Field
152	------  ----  -----
153	0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)
154	4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)
155	8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)
156	12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)
157	16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)
158	17      3     _pad
159	20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))
160	```
161	
162	Each cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`
163	bytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across
164	slots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing
165	sizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows
166	how big it needs the cells.
167	
168	`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation
169	(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`
170	spins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —
171	if contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without
172	changing the API.
173	
174	Writes to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is
175	advanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to
176	see the complete value at the head cell.
177	
178	## Lifetime
179	
180	Slots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live
181	from graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference
182	counting and no end-of-stream propagation — the slot is freed
183	when the run ends, alongside its owning box.
184	
185	Run termination is governed entirely by the pool's active-task
186	counter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further spawns
187	are pending, the run is over. There's nothing the slot store needs
188	to track to make this work.
189	
190	### No wait lists
191	
192	Tasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch
193	layer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they
194	never block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the
195	spawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,
196	no per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.
197	
198	## Backing store
199	
200	Slots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a
201	per-run allocator (described under "Allocation strategy" below) that
202	hands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is
203	sufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write
204	it, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.
205	
206	Synchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for
207	header mutations. There is no allocator-wide mutex on the
208	read/write path; only the per-size-class free lists in the
209	allocator have their own locks.
210	
211	## Slot creation
212	
213	Slot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph
214	loader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,
215	and parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch
216	layer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —
217	all slots that will ever exist are created up front.
218	
219	```c
220	slot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);
221	```
222	
223	`cell_capacity` and `n_cells` come from compile-time analysis of
224	the graph. Boxes downstream of iterators get larger `n_cells` to
225	absorb the iterator's worst-case backlog.
226	
227	If a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small at runtime
228	(producer outpaces consumer beyond the pre-allocation), the slot's
229	ring grows — see "Allocation strategy" below.
230	
231	## C API surface
232	
233	```c
234	slot_id_t slot_alloc       (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells, int flags);
235	void      slot_push        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size, uint32_t tag);
236	int       slot_peek        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // 1-cell: read without draining
237	int       slot_pop         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // N-cell: drain head (or lowest-tag)
238	uint32_t  slot_read_inc    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);            // SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER only
239	int       slot_has_value   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);                          // for spawn-rule check
240	```
241	
242	Flags include:
243	- `SLOT_TAGGED`: cells carry ordering tags; `slot_pop` returns the
244	  lowest-tag cell.
245	- `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`: slot holds a single atomic uint32; reads
246	  via `slot_read_inc` only. `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop`
247	  are not valid on atomic-counter slots.
248	
249	Push always takes a `tag` argument; untagged slots ignore it (or
250	treat 0 as "no order").
251	
252	1-cell peek slot use: producer `push` once at startup (literal) or
253	when its single invocation completes (single-push wire). All
254	consumer tasks `peek` to read the value as many times as their box
255	runs. The cell is never empty after the initial push.
256	
257	N-cell pop slot use: producers `push` repeatedly. Consumer tasks
258	`pop` one cell each. For tagged slots, `pop` returns the
259	lowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO. Pop on an empty slot is a
260	bug — the spawn rule guarantees the slot is non-empty before a
261	task spawns.
262	
263	There is no `slot_ref` / `slot_unref` — slot lifetime is the run.
264	
265	## Submission timing
266	
267	Tasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes. Each box
268	has small per-box state used by the dispatch layer:
269	
270	```
271	box_runtime_state {
272	    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)
273	    int        *port_modes;      // PEEK or POP, per input port
274	    int         n_inputs;
275	    slot_id_t   counter_slot;    // iterator only: SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER slot;
276	                                 // 0 / unused otherwise
277	};
278	```
279	
280	The spawning rule:
281	- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the
282	  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot have a value
283	  available?** "Available" means:
284	  - For peek-mode (1-cell) slots: cell has been written at least
285	    once. Once a peek slot is filled, it stays available — every
286	    subsequent spawn-check on this box passes the peek-port check.
287	  - For pop-mode (N-cell) slots: queue is non-empty.
288	- If yes, spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool. The
289	  task pops (or peeks) one value from each input slot when it
290	  runs.
291	- Each push that completes the input set triggers exactly one
292	  spawn. Multiple pushes accumulate in pop slots; each pop
293	  consumes one, and if more remain, the next push (or check)
294	  re-fires the spawn rule.
295	
296	This makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate
297	in pop slots (possibly multiple per slot), and one task per
298	accumulated value gets spawned.
299	
300	Tasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are
301	ready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking
302	machinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the
303	synchronization primitive.
304	
305	The pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate "blocked
306	tasks" structure.
307	
308	## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback
309	
310	The slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is
311	analyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the
312	graph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each
313	queued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue
314	depth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.
315	
316	Variable-size and unknown-size payloads (a long LLM response, an
317	array whose length is not known until runtime) are handled by a
318	separate **large-value heap** described below — not by allocating
319	huge slots up front.
320	
321	### The lists
322	Each size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly
323	that size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots
324	to cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the
325	run if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.
326	
327	Each list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different
328	size classes never contend with each other.
329	
330	### Allocation
331	Given a request for size N bytes:
332	1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.
333	2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.
334	3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.
335	4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.
336	   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual
337	   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that
338	   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation
339	   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.
340	5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the
341	   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that
342	   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return
343	   the combined chunk.
344	6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see "Growth" below) and
345	   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.
346	7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the
347	   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the
348	   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks
349	   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it
350	   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than
351	   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's
352	   fine.
353	
354	### Deallocation
355	When refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's
356	free list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:
357	check the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge
358	them and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.
359	This is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps
360	small-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred
361	cleanup task to run.
362	
363	### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)
364	Coalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in
365	memory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.
366	
367	Two viable representations:
368	
369	- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in
370	  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.
371	  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.
372	- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start
373	  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and
374	  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to
375	  scan.
376	
377	The linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for
378	splits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows
379	list traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary
380	index — the API doesn't change.
381	
382	### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)
383	
384	For values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM
385	responses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound
386	is not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value
387	directly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:
388	
389	```
390	{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }
391	```
392	
393	`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a
394	plain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.
395	When a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:
396	1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.
397	2. Writes the bytes there.
398	3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.
399	
400	The consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,
401	copies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's
402	refcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the
403	large-value-heap region.
404	
405	The slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.
406	The two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still
407	supporting unbounded outputs.
408	
409	A box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as
410	"variable-size" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the
411	fixed-size path with no indirection.
412	
413	### Growth
414	When all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy
415	a request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,
416	dividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class
417	lists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access
418	to slot memory.
419	
420	### Why this design
421	- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single
422	  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.
423	- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the
424	  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply
425	  not split.
426	- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,
427	  and it costs nothing on the common path.
428	- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never
429	  fires.
430	
431	## No type tags
432	
433	Slots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer
434	reads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business
435	on each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's
436	compiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at
437	build time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not
438	need to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything
439	else. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.
440	
441	## Suggested implementation sequence
442	1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.
443	2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,
444	   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.
445	3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer
446	   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.
447	4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at
448	   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.
449	
450	## Relevant files
451	- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region
452	- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)
453	- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle
454	- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots
455	- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that
456	  ring-buffer slots implement
457	- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2
458	
```

12	## Concept
13	
14	The task dispatch layer is the C component that runs inside each pool
15	worker. The pool calls a single C action — `dispatch_action` — per
16	task. That action is the one place in the runtime that:
17	
18	- Reads from and writes to slots
19	- Calls `lang_spec->invoke`
20	- Picks the output branch per `routing.kind` (issue 233)
21	- Pushes the function's output to the picked branch's downstream
22	  input slots, triggering downstream task spawns
23

25	is replaced wholesale.

27	## Task struct
28	
29	A task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. Its struct carries
30	just the box ID:
31	
32	```c
33	typedef struct {
34	    int  box_id;          // index into the graph's box array
35	} dispatch_task_t;
36	```
37	
38	There is no per-task counter. Iterator counter state lives in a
39	`SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot owned by the box (see issue 302); the
40	action reads and atomically increments it via `slot_read_inc`
41	when it needs the routing index.
42	
43	There is no `input_slots` or `output_slot` array on the task —
44	the box's input slots are durable per-box state (see issue 302).
45	The action looks them up through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.
46	
47	Output is a routing event, not a stored value. When the action
48	finishes, it pushes copies of the return value into the input
49	slots of every downstream box wired to this output (or only the
50	matching branch for comparators and iterators).
51	
52	Tasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's "spawn on input ready"
53	rule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`
54	on the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID. The
55	action's first read of the input slots is what drains them — pop
56	or peek one cell per input port, per the port's mode.

58	## The dispatch action
59	
60	```c
61	action_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);
62	```
63	
64	Phases, in order:
65	
66	### 1. Read inputs into byte buffers
67	
68	Tasks are spawned only when every input port has a value
69	available (issue 302's spawn-on-input-ready rule), so the action
70	does not need to check or block — input availability is the spawn
71	precondition.
72	
73	For each input port:
74	- **Peek-mode (1-cell) port**: `slot_peek` into a heap buffer.
75	  The cell is not drained; subsequent tasks on this box read the
76	  same value.
77	- **Pop-mode (N-cell) port**: `slot_pop` into a heap buffer. One
78	  cell drains; values queued behind it remain. For tagged slots,
79	  pop returns the lowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO.
80	
81	Variable-size payloads work via the large-value heap (issue 302):
82	the cell holds a `{size, offset}` handle that points into the
83	heap; the spec follows the handle if it needs the bytes.
84	
85	Buffers are freed when the action ends.
86	
87	### 3. Dispatch is uniform across routing kinds
88	
89	Every call box runs its function (phase 4) and pushes the
90	function's output (phase 5). The only thing that varies is which
91	downstream branch receives the push (phase 5b — the branch-pick).
92	
93	Boxes carry an optional `routing` field (issue 233):
94	- No `routing`: plain call. Function runs; output fans to all
95	  outgoing wires unconditionally.
96	- `routing.kind: "comparator"`: function runs; output is
97	  compared to `comparand`; only the matching `lt` / `eq` / `gt`
98	  branch fires.
99	- `routing.kind: "iterator"`: function runs; output is routed to
100	  `outputs[slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)]`.
101	- `routing.kind: "randomizer" / "weighted" / "distributor"`:
102	  function runs; output is routed by the kind-specific rule.

104	The function always runs. There is no "iterator skips invoke"

113	Call `lang->invoke` with:
114	- `handle` — the per-worker language runtime state

116	- `input_data[]`, `input_sizes[]` — pointers and sizes for each

141	
142	The action picks the branch (or branches) and pushes the

145	- **No routing field** (plain call): push to every outgoing

147	- **comparator**: compare output to `comparand`, push to the

155	For routing kinds that derive an order tag (iterator,
156	randomizer, weighted), the push carries `tag = idx` so consumers

159	After each push, the spawn-on-input-ready check (issue 302) fires
160	on the receiving box. If that push completes its input set, a

164	
165	Slots are durable for the run; tasks don't unref. Run termination

181	## Initial submission
182	
183	At startup, the pool runner walks the graph and pushes the
184	literal-input values (from `value` fields on input ports) directly
185	into the corresponding input slots. Boxes whose input set becomes
186	fully populated by literals — entry-point boxes — immediately
187	satisfy the spawn-on-input-ready condition, and their first task
188	gets queued. From there, every subsequent task spawn follows from
189	the regular phase-5 push → spawn-check chain.
190	
191	Iterator counter state starts at 0; literal-only entry iterators
192	spawn their first task at startup and increment from there.
193	
194	## Iterator counter and parallel iteration
195	
196	The iterator's counter lives in a `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot
197	allocated for the box at graph load time (issue 302). The
198	dispatch action reads and increments it atomically, mid-action:
199	
200	```c
201	uint32_t branch_idx = slot_read_inc(box->counter_slot, n_iter_outputs);
202	slot_push(downstream[branch_idx].input_slot, output_buf, output_size,
203	          /* tag = */ branch_idx);
204	```
205	
206	`slot_read_inc` returns the current counter value `mod
207	n_iter_outputs` and atomically advances the underlying counter.
208	Concurrent iterator tasks on different workers each call
209	`slot_read_inc` independently and each get a unique value —
210	**iterator tasks parallelize across workers**, picking distinct
211	branches without coordination.
212	
213	No box-side mutable state, no per-task counter snapshot. The
214	counter is just data in a slot the dispatch layer reads.
215	
216	## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration
217	
218	With parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is
219	non-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C
220	before task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop
221	at C would consume them out of iteration order.
222	
223	The fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase
224	5) carries the counter value the action read for this invocation:
225	
226	```c
227	slot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,
228	          /* tag = */ branch_idx_or_counter_snapshot);
229	```
230	
231	Consumer slots downstream of iterators are allocated with the
232	`SLOT_TAGGED` flag (issue 302). `slot_pop` on a tagged slot
233	returns the cell with the lowest tag — preserving iterator-counter
234	order regardless of push race.
235	
236	Compile-time analysis decides which slots are tagged: any slot
237	whose feeding wire originates (transitively, through a fan-out
238	chain) at an iterator branch gets tagged. Slots not downstream of
239	iterators are untagged and pop FIFO at no extra cost.
240	
241	Plain-call and comparator pushes carry tag = 0 (or the snapshot of
242	their own iterator-ancestor's counter, if applicable, propagated
243	through their phase-5 pushes). Tags compose naturally through
244	multi-hop chains.
245	
246	### Cross-iterator pairing of multiple iterator inputs
247	
248	When non-iterator consumer C has two input ports wired from two
249	different iterators A and B, each input port has its own tagged
250	queue. Both queues pop in tag order independently:
251	- C's task K pops the K-th tag from A's queue (which equals A's
252	  K-th invocation's value).
253	- The same K-th tag from B's queue.
254	
255	Pairing by tag = `(A_K, B_K)` for every K, deterministic
256	regardless of which iterator's tasks run faster.
257	
258	## Routing kinds (issue 233)
259	
260	Every call box runs its function. Routing kinds differ only in
261	how the function's output is dispatched to downstream
262	connections:
263	
264	| `routing.kind`   | Output ports        | Branch picker                                                |
265	|------------------|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
266	| (absent / plain) | single port         | fan to all outgoing connections                              |
267	| `comparator`     | `lt` / `eq` / `gt`  | compare(output, comparand) → lt/eq/gt                        |
268	| `iterator`       | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, N)`                             |
269	| `randomizer`     | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | `hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % N`                 |
270	| `weighted`       | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | cumulative-band lookup against a counter scaled to PRECISION |
271	| `distributor`    | `out_0` … `out_N-1` | argmin over downstream slot fill levels                      |
272	
273	Plain call (no `routing` field) skips the branch picker entirely
274	— phase 5 fans the output to all wires. The function still runs
275	the same as for any branched call. Issue 233 carries the schema
276	and the per-kind UI.
277	
278	## Open questions
279	
280	(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)
281	
282	- Output buffer sizing: heap-allocated to the box's declared output
283	  size at runtime. No fixed cap. Variable-size outputs go through the
284	  large-value heap (issue 302).
285	- Queued-input slot lifetime: producers hold refs while alive,
286	  consumer holds a ref while consuming, slot freed when all drop.
287	  References are the producer-liveness tracking mechanism.
288	- Comparator output encoding: dispatch layer handles comparison
289	  semantics directly. No spec involvement, no encoded "branch tag" in
290	  the slot — the branch is a routing-time value computed by the
291	  dispatch layer from the input.
292

2	
3	## Status

6	## Current behavior
7	The executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a

10	
11	## Phase model
12	
13	Phase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development
14	target while editor work is in progress.
15	
16	Phase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going
17	forward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an
18	alternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner
19	replaces it. There is no "fallback to synchronous" mode.
20	
21	### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface
22	
23	The following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:
24	
25	| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |
26	|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
27	| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |
28	| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |
29	| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |
30	| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |
31	
32	All threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to
33	the pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or
34	dispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,
35	on equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.
36	
37	## Intended behavior
38	
39	### Pool source
40	The thread pool is **SoraMech-owned**, written from scratch under
41	`libs/task-pool/`. The 3d-rts pool at
42	`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`
43	is the **design reference**, not a dependency. We need full control
44	over the spawn primitive, the worker context, the init barrier
45	(below), and iterator-pinning extensions — all reasons not to inherit
46	an external implementation.
47	
48	The pool exposes (at minimum):
49	
50	```c
51	pool_t *pool_create(int n_workers);
52	void    pool_destroy(pool_t *p);
53	void    pool_spawn(pool_t *p, action_fn_t fn, void *arg);
54	void    pool_wait_quiescent(pool_t *p);   // blocks until active count hits zero
55	void    pool_init_barrier(pool_t *p);     // see "Init barrier" below
56	```
57	
58	3d-rts's frame-ring + park-on-slot machinery is referenced for
59	patterns; we don't reimplement features we don't need.
60	
61	### Where the pool lives in the process
62	The pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map
63	run. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and
64	destroyed after the run completes.
65	
66	The C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):
67	
68	```c
69	int main(int argc, char **argv) {
70	    // 1. parse map path from argv
71	    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)
72	    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses
73	    // 4. allocate per-input-port slots for every box (issue 302)
74	    // 5. pool = pool_create(n_workers)
75	    // 6. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present
76	    // 7. pool_init_barrier(pool)  ← block until every worker is fully initialized
77	    // 8. push every input port's literal value into its slot
78	    // 9. spawn tasks for boxes whose input set is now satisfied
79	    // 10. pool_wait_quiescent(pool)
80	    // 11. write last-run.jsonl
81	    // 12. pool_destroy(pool)
82	}
83	```
84	
85	### Init barrier
86	
87	Workers are not safe to dispatch tasks to until **every worker has
88	fully completed init for every language spec the map uses**. If the
89	main thread spawns a task before a worker's `lua_State` is up, the
90	task lands on a null handle.
91	
92	`pool_init_barrier` is the join point:
93	
94	1. Each worker's startup runs all `lang->init(worker_idx)` calls in
95	   a defined order, populating its `worker_ctx_t.handles[]`.
96	2. After completing its inits, each worker increments a shared
97	   atomic `workers_ready` counter and blocks on a condition
98	   variable.
99	3. The main thread waits until `workers_ready == n_workers`.
100	4. Main thread broadcasts the condition variable; all workers
101	   release simultaneously and begin pulling tasks.
102	
103	This is a one-shot barrier — it runs once at pool startup. After
104	quiescence it doesn't re-engage; teardown takes a different path.
105	
106	The barrier also protects against partial init failures: if any
107	worker's `init` returns an error, the barrier never completes and
108	the main thread can detect it via a timeout or per-worker status
109	flag.
110	
111	### Graph loading: ported to C
112	The graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives
113	inside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no
114	embedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small
115	vendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to
116	implementation).
117	
118	Lua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even
119	then, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool
120	runner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.
121	
122	### Per-worker language runtimes
123	No language is treated as the "native" or preferred language at the
124	thread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the
125	same task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's
126	invocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.
127	
128	Each worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per
129	language it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool
130	startup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:
131	
132	```c
133	typedef struct {
134	    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state
135	    int     thread_idx;
136	} worker_ctx_t;
137	```
138	
139	Only the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.
140	If the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any
141	worker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and
142	passes that set to the pool runner at startup.
143	
144	The per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language
145	runtime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`
146	function at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.
147	
148	### Worker context access
149	Worker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread
150	worker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after
151	the thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.
152	
153	### Pool size
154	Number of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs
155	(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum
156	(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment
157	variable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.
158	
159	### Slots are owned by input ports (issue 302)
160	Each box has one ring-buffer slot per input port, allocated at
161	graph load time and durable for the run. The pool runner walks
162	every box during the load step and populates a per-box slot table.
163	Slots are not allocated per-task; tasks pop and push but never
164	allocate. See issue 302 for the slot lifecycle and lifetime model.
165	
166	### Quiescence
167	The runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`
168	and decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits
169	on a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.
170	
171	This naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each
172	re-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. When the
173	counter reaches zero, the run is over.
174	
175	Deadlock is not a concern at runtime. The graph validator (running at
176	load) rejects non-iterator cycles and inputs without producers. Errors
177	inside a task crash the program (issue 303), so there is no
178	half-completed-producer case to worry about. An iterator parking
179	because its upstream queue is empty is not deadlock — it is the
180	natural end-of-stream condition; once the active-task counter reaches
181	zero with the iterator parked, the run ends cleanly.
182
